newsitem.title: USA: Magnesium stocks headed lower, all eyes on bevcans.
newsitem.headline: Magnesium stocks headed lower, all eyes on bevcans.

text.p: Magnesium inventories are likely to show a drop in the first quarter, but the market was still anxiously waiting to see how aluminum beverage canmaking shapes up over coming months, producer officials said.

"I think shipments in the first quarter are going to run at close to record levels," Howard Kaplan of Magnesium Corp said. "But the biggest issue facing the industry is to what degree and how fast will aluminum cans recover or not."
Magnesium is added to aluminum which is rolled into canstock for making beverage cans. Last year the amount of magnesium used in alloying aluminum fell 15 percent, Kaplan said.

Aluminum industry analyst Stewart Spector said the rise of the PET plastic bottle stunted growth in the aluminum beverage can in soft drinks, and more and more people were drinking imported or independently-made (micro-brewery) beers which are often packaged in bottles.
Aluminum sheet for cans also become thinner, using less metal to make.
"There will be further lightweighting over the next couple of years," Spector said.

Recently Pechiney SA said its U.S. beverage canmaking subsidiary, American National Can, will shut two or three plants this year due to overcapacity in the industry and tough competition from plastic bottles in the U.S.

But one trader was already seeing an improvement in magnesium offtake for the canstock sector in the past month. "Some of the (aluminum) producers are doing some tolling because they cannot handle it (canstock orders) all," he said.
Other merchants saw no real recovery in canstock so far.
Spot primary magnesium prices in the U.S. were quoted from $1.32 to $1.38 per pound, with traders differing on whether tags are firming.
Both Kaplan and Robert Edgar of Hydro Magnesium, part of Norway's Norsk Hydro said magnesium inventories have levelled off.
The International Magnesium Association reported that inventory at the end of 1996 stood at 42,100 tonnes, up 19,300 tonnes from the end of 1995.
"They are probably a little bit on the high side but not really awful," Edgar said.
Figures for the first quarter this year are due within a few weeks.

Ukraine's Kalush producer was set to produce about 9,000 tonnes of primary magnesium this year, sharply down from about 17,000 tonnes in 1996, industry sources said. Kalush was looking to diversify production after its magnesium exports were hit by duties in the European Union.

But supply pipeline stocks were down to normal levels and the seasonal effects of the canning sheet were coming in, Edgar added. "The business level has improved enough that it might just either stop the build up or pull it back a little."
Kaplan said:"I expect to see inventories come down a little bit."
